newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: RUGBY UNION-DUTCH TEAM HOPE TO EMULATE CRICKETERS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-DUTCH TEAM HOPE TO EMULATE CRICKETERS.

text.p: Although rugby union is a fringe sport in the soccer-mad Netherlands, the sport's bosses are confident the national side can emulate the Dutch cricket team and win a World Cup place.
Only last year, former national coach John van Altena described the Netherlands' prospects of getting through to the 1999 World Cup finals in Wales as "laughable and unrealistic".

But Dutch hopes have been raised not only by moves to expand the tournament to 20 nations from 16, but by their own determination to put the sport on a professional footing plus the appointment of former New Zealand All Black Geoff Old as national coach to replace the unambitious Van Altena.
"We want to qualify and participate in the 1999 World Cup. That's the target," Old said after his second squad session.
Old is neither the first full-time, nor the first foreign coach as Englishman Dennis Power managed the side in the 1960s.

But the selection of one of a handful of New Zealand coaches with a national coaching qualification is a big step for a small rugby nation and a measure of its intent to launch the domestic game into the top flight.

The Netherlands Rugby Board (NRB) and Old teamed up at the suggestion of the game's ruling body, the International Rugby Football Board (IRFB). The Dutch were also able to draw "a reasonable sum of money" from the IRFB's development fund.
The appointment of Old is the most high profile change, but not the only one. The NRB says it has transformed itself from an old boy's club to a full-time professional body.

It says it is no longer prepared for players to stumble into the sport from its traditional university recruiting grounds. From this year it is actively going out to preach the rugby message to youngsters at school.
"The board has restructured. I'm just part of the equation," Old said in an interview.

Next month, construction of a new national stadium in Amsterdam is due to start. The 1,600-seater stand is modest compared with recent developments at London's Twickenham and plans for Cardiff's Arms Park, but will be a vast improvement on the national side's nomadic treks round club grounds.
"They'll have a home, something to identify with," says Old.
The ground will be part-funded by the Dutch national lottery with additional sponsorship from brewing giant Heineken, which already sponsors top-class rugby in Wales.
Dutch club sides are also succeeding in minor European competition. The Hague, national league leaders, convincingly beat Belgian and German club opposition earlier this year.
"The other target is to widen the base of the pyramid...we hope we'll have 25,000 members after the year 2000," said NRB director Peter Bus.

About 9,000 now play the game, but clubs are expanding and social sides of limbering locals are swelling bar profits. In the top teams, only a sprinkling of experienced expatriates oust the local talent available. Unlike the national cricket eleven, the Dutch rugby XV are indeed Dutch. Their only innate Dutch deficiency, they say, is a passion for arguing on the pitch.
Old's appointment has led to a rash of articles in the normally indifferent Dutch media, although most had to explain that the All Blacks are "one of the best teams in the world".
Old heads back home to New Zealand in January, but both he and the NRB hope to extend his contract to three years soon.
The New Zealander says he is encouraged by what he has seen so far,
The willingness to learn is an asset, he says, but the team must work harder.
"Basically the game is the same anywhere in the world. The skill level (here) is lacking a little..., but possibly it all comes down to the fact that the players aren't fit."
"If you fix the fitness problem, then the skill level will naturally rise."

Old's first training session -- a light Sunday run-out, a clash of "Probables" and "Possibles" in the morning and a squad session in the afternoon -- continued until sunset under the gaze of Old's wife.
"They work them hard in New Zealand," she explained.
Remedial work is essential.
The Netherlands' first foray this season ended ignominiously with a 20-15 home defeat to Tunisia on a rain-soaked pitch last month but many Dutch supporters considered this an aberration.
"The conditions were terrible. They just coped better," said one rugby board member.
A Dutch side depleted by injury then lost 55-11 to Portugal.

Dutch rugby's toughest task may is more long-term: widening its appeal of rugby beyond its traditional student footholds and convincing youngsters that the route to sporting glory lies in the footsteps of David Campese and Will Carling rather than those of national idols like Johan Cruyff, Ruud Gullit and Patrick Kluivert.
"That's the competition we're up against," says Bus.
